## Removal Is Measurement, Run Backward

The dependence chapter asked *how much* two variables move together.  This
chapter asked how to *cancel* that movement.  They are the same object seen
from two sides:

| | [Measure](../dependence/index.qmd) (Ch. 1) | Remove (Ch. 4) |
|---|---|---|
| Question | how dependent are $X$ and $Y$? | make $\hat y$ independent of $S$ |
| Tool | a dependence measure $\operatorname{Dep}$ | the *same* measure, as a penalty |
| Output | a number | a model on the trade-off frontier |

Every rung of the removal ladder is a measurement rung used as a loss:

$$
\text{loss} = \text{fit}(\hat y, y) +
\mu \cdot \underbrace{\operatorname{Dep}(\hat y, S)}_{\text{a Ch.-1 measure, differentiated}}
$$

And the failures map across too.  Pearson's blindness to curves
(measurement) *is* linear neutrality's hole (removal).  The histogram's
curse of dimensionality (measurement) *is* why density-based removal needs
[Gaussianization](../gaussianization/index.qmd).  If a measure cannot *see*
a shape of dependence, no penalty built on it can *remove* that shape.

## The Two Roads, Once More

The dependence chapter's fork — *do you need the distribution?* — reappears,
now about *removing* rather than measuring:

```{python}
#| label: fig-two-roads-removal
#| fig-cap: "The removal decision tree — the dependence chapter's fork, run in reverse. Both branches end at a neutral model; only the right branch needs a density, and only its conditional form yields a fair predictor."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 5))
ax.axis("off")

nodes = {
    "q":   (0.50, 0.90, "Make ŷ independent of S",            14, INK),
    "q1":  (0.50, 0.68, "Do you need the density?",            12, INK),
    "r1a": (0.18, 0.46, "NO → kernel removal\n"
                        "Dep = CKA / HSIC(ŷ, S)",              11, COOL),
    "r1b": (0.82, 0.46, "YES → information removal\n"
                        "Dep = MI / total correlation",         11, WARM),
    "r2a": (0.18, 0.18, "differentiable · bounded\n"
                        "no density needed\n"
                        "(the workhorse — keras-fairkl)",       10, COOL),
    "r2b": (0.60, 0.18, "marginal / joint\nGaussianize\n"
                        "(NOT enough — leaks)",                 10, CRASH),
    "r2c": (0.92, 0.18, "conditional ŷ | S\n"
                        "(genuine independence,\n"
                        "needs the density)",                   10, GREEN),
}

for key, (x0, y0, text, fs, col) in nodes.items():
    ax.text(x0, y0, text, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, color=col,
            fontweight="bold" if key in ("q", "q1") else "normal",
            bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.4", fc="white", ec=col, lw=1.4))

arrow_kw = dict(arrowstyle="->", lw=1.4, color=INK)
for (x0, y0), (x1, y1) in [
    ((0.50, 0.85), (0.50, 0.74)),
    ((0.50, 0.63), (0.22, 0.52)),
    ((0.50, 0.63), (0.78, 0.52)),
    ((0.18, 0.40), (0.18, 0.25)),
    ((0.82, 0.40), (0.63, 0.25)),
    ((0.82, 0.40), (0.90, 0.25)),
]:
    ax.annotate("", xy=(x1, y1), xytext=(x0, y0),
                xycoords="axes fraction", textcoords="axes fraction",
                arrowprops=arrow_kw)

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The kernel road is the practical default — differentiable, bounded,
density-free.  The information road reconnects fairness to
[Gaussianization](../gaussianization/index.qmd), with one sharp caveat the
[Gaussianize-first lab](labs/lab-tool2.5-gaussianize-first.qmd) proves:
marginal or joint Gaussianization is *not* enough; only the **conditional**
transform — Gaussianize $\hat y$ *given* $S$ — yields a fair model.

## What Each Rung Can Cancel

```{python}
#| label: fig-shape-removed
#| fig-cap: "What each rung can cancel. Drop removes nothing (proxies leak); linear removes the line; CKA and adversarial remove line and curve. Pick the cheapest Dep that sees what you fear — the same advice as the measurement ladder, mirrored."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.6))
rungs = ["drop\nfeature", "linear\n(cka_linear)", "CKA\n(cka_rbf)",
         "adversarial"]
removes_line = [0, 1, 1, 1]
removes_curve = [0, 0, 1, 1]
xpos = np.arange(len(rungs))
ax.bar(xpos - 0.18, removes_line, width=0.36, color=COOL, label="removes the line")
ax.bar(xpos + 0.18, removes_curve, width=0.36, color=CRASH,
       label="removes the curve")
ax.set_xticks(xpos); ax.set_xticklabels(rungs, fontsize=10)
ax.set_yticks([0, 1]); ax.set_yticklabels(["no", "yes"])
ax.set_title("Pick the cheapest Dep that sees what you fear", fontsize=12)
ax.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="center right")
despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## The Through-Line
The **transform** that threads the measurement ladder threads this one too:
a hand-picked map (ranks, kernels) on the no-density road, a learned
invertible map (Gaussianization) on the density road.  Measuring it,
removing it, and *propagating* it are
[one operation seen three ways](../uncertainty/05-predictive-bands.qmd#the-capstone--one-machine-three-uses).
:::

## Hand-Off

You can now force a model to be blind to a chosen variable — fairness and
factor-neutrality, one operation.  The companion move is to stop *removing*
dependence and start **propagating** it: carrying uncertainty and risk
through a model, where the same Gaussianization machine runs *backward* to
generate scenarios.  See [Uncertainty](../uncertainty/index.qmd).

The hands-on [labs](labs/index.qmd) put all of this on real data: a credit
model neutralized against `sex`, and a strategy neutralized against the
market — with the identical objective, and the identical code.
